div.p: This part of the training aims at introducing the basic technical concepts in Odoo: fields, models, relationships between models, and different views. Understanding these elements will help you analyze hidden links between applications, identify mechanisms behind views, and find workarounds for non-standard flows. If no workaround exists, you’ll be able to design the required functional flow for development.

While we remain functional business analysts and project leaders (not technical consultants), speaking the same technical language is crucial. Don’t worry if some aspects feel challenging—learning through experience is key!

p.span: is a code hosting platform for version control and collaboration. It lets you and others work together on projects from anywhere.

div.p: When we thought about creating a PaaS platform after we already had a SaaS, we decided that we would hook to Github tools and that Odoo.sh would receive notifications from Github and act accordingly. For example:

ul.li: everytime a new branch is created on Odoo.sh, it will create it on your Github repo (if you have the access rights)
When a new commit is pushed to an existing branch, Odoo.sh will update the build of that branch or recreate a new build.

p.span: Also, thanks to this integration, you have a clear history and you can easily push developments from your repository to the development branch.

button.class: accordion-header accordion-button gap-2 bg-transparent h6-fs fw-bold text-decoration-none text-reset transition-none justify-content-between collapsed

p.span: The host locations (where the data is stored) are America , Europe and Asia. The choice of this location will have an impact on the latency of the requests.
You must consider where the internal users and the possible website visitors are located in order to choose the host location that fits your company the best.

button.class: accordion-header accordion-button gap-2 bg-transparent h6-fs fw-bold text-decoration-none text-reset transition-none justify-content-between collapsed

div.p: A repository is usually used to organize a single project. Repositories can contain folders and files, images, videos, spreadsheets, and data sets – anything your project needs. It’s hosted on Github. The repository can either be hosted on the client’s github account or on Odoo’s.

ul.li: Odoo performs the developments.
The client cannot develop themselves.
It means that we have total control of every line of code related to the project and we can maintain and upgrade the database efficiently since we know what's in it.

p.strong: If the partner hosts the repository themselves:

ul.li: Odoo will not develop anything and reject requests to do so.
The partner will perform all developments
We will not maintain any developments done in the repository.

p.strong: What if the repo is transferred to the client from Odoo?

ul.li: As soon as we transfer the ownership of the repository to the customer, we will no longer maintain any custom code and it is now the customers responsibility to do so moving forward.

p.strong: What if the repo is transferred to Odoo from the client?

ul.li: We will perform a review of all developments as well as their code and rewrite code if necessary in order to maintain what has been done.
We will then bill the client 1 years worth of maintenance for every line of code.

button.class: accordion-header accordion-button gap-2 bg-transparent h6-fs fw-bold text-decoration-none text-reset transition-none justify-content-between collapsed

div.p: Branching is a way to work on different versions of a repository at the same time.
By default your repository has one branch named master which is considered to be the definitive branch. We use branches to experiment and make changes before committing them to master.

ul.li: Production: Sometimes called “Master”
Copies of the production database
Custom code available for testing
Each staging branch must be bought
Demo data only
Free

div.p: When you create a new branch from the master branch, you’re making a copy, or snapshot, of the master branch as it was at that moment in time. If someone else makes changes to the master branch while you were working on your branch you can pull in those updates if you wish.
Have you ever saved different versions of a file? Something like:

ul.li: story.txt
story-joe-edit.txt
story-joe-edit-reviewed.txt

div.p: Branches accomplish similar goals in GitHub repositories.
Here at Odoo, our developers use branches for keeping bug fixes and feature work separate from our master (production) branch. When a change is ready, they merge their branch into master.

button.class: accordion-header accordion-button gap-2 bg-transparent h6-fs fw-bold text-decoration-none text-reset transition-none justify-content-between collapsed

span.p: How do we move from one branch to another in the middle of development ?

ol.li: Development : This environment is where the development is tested with Demo Data. Once the branch is green the development can be moved into Staging.
Staging : Is the QA testing branch that groups together different development branches so that we test the combined features on a copy of the production database. → Integration testing.
Production : Once the development is stable, tested and validated by the customer in Staging, the developer can then push the changes into the production database.

div.p: Here a small reminder of the implementation scheme on Odoo.sh:

button.class: accordion-header accordion-button gap-2 bg-transparent h6-fs fw-bold text-decoration-none text-reset transition-none justify-content-between collapsed

div.p: On GitHub saved changes are called commits.
Each commit has an associated commit message which is a description explaining why a particular change was made.
Commit messages capture the history of your changes so other contributors can understand what you’ve done and why.

button.class: accordion-header accordion-button gap-2 bg-transparent h6-fs fw-bold text-decoration-none text-reset transition-none justify-content-between collapsed

div.p: Pull Requests (PR) are the heart of collaboration on GitHub.
When you open a pull request, you’re proposing your changes and requesting that someone review and pull in your contribution and merge them into their branch.
Pull requests show diffs, or differences, of the content from both branches. The changes, additions, and subtractions are shown in green and red.

button.class: accordion-header accordion-button gap-2 bg-transparent h6-fs fw-bold text-decoration-none text-reset transition-none justify-content-between collapsed

div.p: Builds show the status of the update we have performed. The builds help us to test the behavior of the server. The build creation is considered as successful if there are no errors. The build status can easily be identified using the following colors.

Red color indicates that our updates have some errors which in turn leads to an unsuccessful build.
Orange color indicates a warning. So this shows that the build is almost successful. You can fix these warning messages to create a successful build.
Green color indicates the successful creation of a build.
You can also rebuild a branch using the Rebuild icon.
It is important to know that:

ul.li: Staging branch will last for 1 months.
Development branch will last for 3 days.

button.class: accordion-header accordion-button gap-2 bg-transparent h6-fs fw-bold text-decoration-none text-reset transition-none justify-content-between collapsed

p.span: The production database workers define how many concurrent requests can be handled simultaneously, so the workload that it can handle . It is necessary to have enough workers to serve all incoming requests as they arrive but having more doesn't speed up the requests' processing time.

Typically, we estimate that one worker can manage up to 6 concurrent users. Remember 99% of the time users are probably reading or typing (not clicking buttons) and that doesn't count as 'using' Odoo. In this case, using odoo would only mean clicking a button, running a report, importing data, etc...

span.span: As a rule of thumb, you should count about 1 worker per 25 users or 1 worker for 5000 daily website visitors. It can vary much depending on the database usage and website. The shared offer goes up to 8 workers, beyond this a dedicated server is required.

img.class: img img-fluid mx-auto o_we_custom_image rounded-circle rounded

p.span: Internally, we prefer developing on SH as soon as the development is estimated to be longer than 10 hours or when changes need to be developed for the Website. The developments can be performed in Python, JS and CSS languages and are not restricted to XML or automated and server actions as the source code is no longer shared by all databases and is unique per database.
The platform allows managing the content and developments well in the long run. With the Github integration, the history of all changes made in the code is easily accessible.

The multiple environments offered by Odoo.sh (Production, Staging and development) makes testing new features easier, as it can be tested with test data (in the development environment) and with the production data (in the staging environment).

p.span: First, know that the platform/hosting is also going to have an impact on the approach we have on possible customization and development of the database.

div.p: If you plan to go only for configuration or customization (i.e: use Studio), then we would recommend going on our SaaS. It's very cost efficient, as you won't need the tools to facilitate developments that Odoo.sh provides.

p.span: Keep in mind that only major versions (1x.00) are allowed on SH, while SaaS offers intermediate versions. So if you think that you may do a lot of development, it may be better to start directly on SH (or to start on the last major version on SaaS) as to make the migration possible. Indeed, starting on a SaaS 15.2 for example, wouldn't allow you to go back to Odoo.sh easily. You would have to wait for the Odoo 16 upgrade before you could switch to the Odoo.sh platform.
F

irst, some practical information about Studio. It is an application developed by Odoo that allows you to customize your database. It's a great tool for customization but it remains a functional tool. Since October 2022, there's no difference in cost between using studio or expecting to go for regular development (on .Sh or on premise). So you should rather consider the following:

div.p: - If you only need customizing -> opt for Studio and save hosting and upgrade costs (indeed, changes made with Studio are included in the license).

- If you know you'll need to do a lot of customization and/or development (like changing the business logic or integrating with another software), Odoo.sh or an on premise deployment is the way to go.

div.p: How to's​

div.class: o_wslides_fs_content align-items-stretch justify-content-center d-flex flex-grow-1 order-2
o_wslide_fs_article_content bg-white block w-100 overflow-auto p-3

p.span: Prior to diving head first in a development demand, we would like to remind you that every development should be challenged, as explained in our methodology

p.font: A specification is a written document that describes how a feature has to be developed to meet a customer’s requirement.
You can follow along with the slides :
p.a: Slides | How to Write a Good Spec

div.p: If you are doing a development it is because you have a business need ! You are trying to solve an issue, improve a functionality, etc. because you need it in order to work. As Business Analyst you need to understand where that need comes from and why is it preventing your customer to work properly.

li.p: Understand the need / issue regardless Odoo specificity

ul.li: Standard Solution ?
Workaround ?
Studio ?
Identify the actors impacted
Understand the added value for the client

p.span: In our job we should not agree with customers all the time, but we have to do what's best for them. Being too complacent with customers can lead to unsuccessful implementations, losing focus on priorities, delays and even churns.

li.span: Sometimes, it can happen that our clients are not very familiar yet with their business (e.g.: a client starting a new activity or business, or simply doing something because they have always done it this way). If you notice that some of their requirements don’t make sense don’t hesitate to question their reasoning.

Though you are not an expert of your client’s business processes, you are an Odoo expert with business knowledge that you can use to challenge the client. If you have any concerns don’t hesitate to talk to your team or more experienced consultants.

Keep in mind that clients tend to see dev as necessary just because they want to recreate options they have in their current software. This is never a good reason to start a development. What we do is replace its current ERP, not copy it.

Most of our clients are not tech savvy and have little understanding of the complexity of their requirements and the impact on the structure of their database. For most of our clients this is the first time they implement an ERP and sometimes they forget that the apps are integrated with each other. For this reason a modification in an app can impact another app and has the potential to create issues. What we should do is to explain to them why something is too complicated using simple terms and metaphors. In this way, it’s usually easier to align with them and to make them understand the reason why we say “no” to a development.
We have a technical team who can help us define the complexity and feasibility of a requirement. The input of the technical team can therefore be an excellent tool to challenge the customer.

Don't forget that in principle, doing a development also implies risks : it creates a technical debt, it adds complexities to upgrade/maintain, many times it leads to a delay in the project and it, might be more complex to support. Among the negative aspects, we also find a higher cost for the customer. If required, the financial argument can also be useful, but it is always better to convince with logic than money.

span.style: font-size: medium; background-color: transparent; font-weight: normal;

p.span: When we speak about a standard Odoo solution, we mean that we haven’t done any development, any automated action of the type “execute Python code” and we haven’t changed any record rules. We stick to the Odoo’s apps without doing any kind of modification, only configuration. In general, going for a standard approach will ease the implementation, save time, and then save money for the client. Furthermore, the more standard an implementation will be, the easier it is to maintain. Meaning it will take considerably less time and testing to upgrade to future versions, since every line of code is a potential issue that must be analyzed when upgrading.

Therefore, development should be considered only when a standard solution doesn’t exist or when a standard workaround would add way too much complexity and decrease the usability of the system. Before working on a specification you should be sure all standard possibilities and workarounds have been considered. Ask yourself: “Is the value with the development higher than the cost of the development?”

span.span: If yes, you can consider a development.

p.span: Keep in mind that there is always a trade-off between automation and flexibility. The more you automate processes the less flexible your solution will be. Be sure all aspects of the business (corner cases) have been considered before working on the specification. The development should not be a blocking point for your customer in the future.
It follows that, in some situations, it’s worth challenging your customer when the added value is too low compared to the cost of the development.

Once you are convinced on why to go for a development, you have to ask your customer to validate your business analysis and the functional part too. The validation is always mandatory, to be sure to have really understood which was the issue at stake and why the development is necessary for her.

div.div: A specification is a written document that describes how a feature has to be developed to meet a customer’s requirement.

p.span: Purpose

span.style: font-size: medium; color: rgb(67, 67, 67); font-weight: normal;

b.span: Writing a good specification will make sure that:
The customer, the developer and you are on the same page regarding what needs to be done.
The developer can provide the best estimation and the best solution

div.class: o_editor_banner o_not_editable lh-1 d-flex align-items-center alert alert-info pb-0 pt-3

p.span: The purpose of the specification is to transform the business need into functional/technical requirements that will allow the developer to create the new feature.

button.class: accordion-header accordion-button justify-content-between gap-2 bg-transparent h6-fs fw-bold text-decoration-none text-reset transition-none collapsed

p.span: Imagine that your customer wants to build a house and they share their needs. You, the BA, are the architect. Your role is to understand what he wants, draw how to build it and make the plans for the house. Basically, what you want is that the builder (the developer) understands what’s expected from them and what they should do.

Rather than saying "I need a big window in the kitchen" you will say "I need a lot of light in the kitchen while cooking". The difference here is that you explain why you need light rather than a solution to this requirement.
It's the architect's job to find the best way of doing it based on the different parameters that may have to be taken into consideration.
Specification content

div.p: A specification is composed of 4 different elements: Project Context, Business Need, Functional Specification, Technical Specification.

li.span: What’s the business need? Explain the customer’s need/issue regardless of Odoo specificity.

p.span: When writing the business needs itself, you shouldn’t use bullet points as you were answering the above question - those were just a tool to help you evaluate the issue. The output should be a brief but complete description of the business necessity - without any technical or Odoo terms - which includes all the elements derived from your analysis. It should be clear for anyone without any business knowledge - just like explaining to a 5 years old child.

The purpose of the functional specification is to describe the business necessity and how to handle it in Odoo. If the main question of the previous section was “WHY”, here we are answering “HOW” we solve the issue from a functional perspective. The goal is to “translate” the business necessity in a more functional language - using Odoo terms and flow - in order to pass the information we gathered during our meetings to developers and technical consultants. You should use technical terms for fields and models.
You can organize your functional specification in 3 sections :

li.span: HOW : Explanation of the way Odoo can handle the business need
In the standard solution, where would we change something (AS IS)

div.p: Try to be visual as much as possible by using screenshots. At Odoo we use excalidraw as tool to draw and map our solutions.

p.span: This part is not your responsibility, but it will be written by a technical consultant based on your functional specification. This section aims to answer the question: “HOW do you solve the issue in Odoo (in depth)?”
They will take into account Data structure, Views, Method to redefine, JavaScript, …. And make an estimation of the time it will take to make the development.

You will receive the estimation of the time needed. Share this information with your customer to receive the validation and then you can proceed with the development. This estimation is not binding and it usually comes with a reliability ratio, a probability stating we’ll stay within the initially planned hours for the dev (EX: the dev will take 30 hrs at 90% reliability level). In other words, it means that sometimes the developer uses more hours than the ones initially planned. Do not forget neither that reliability also means that we can fail... And not deliver anything. This is totally normal and your customer should be aware of this possibility.

p.font: Note: the perfect specification doesn't exist! BUT a good functional specification:

li.span: Is consistent with the business need
Every aspect of the functional specification should find its justification in the description of the problem to solve
Contains a detailed description on how you will solve the issue using Odoo
Takes into account both the main use case and also possible corner cases. This point is particularly important, especially when testing.

p.span: Always include screenshots of your test database, flowchart or any other tool which helps to visualize the client’s business flow or the process in Odoo

li.span: Make sure you’re aware of the differences between a model and a view
Use the technical name of models and fields to help developers better understand what you mean. To read the name of fields remember to go into developer mode.

p.span: When you want to add a field make sure you write down:

span.span: The field type (char, int, float, text…)

li.span: Do not mention any method, action, etc.. names in this part. Just write in Odoo terms, there’s no need for technical terms. The developers are there to help us with their expertise to find the best method, action, etc.. for your development.

ul.li: A good practice is to add the necessary steps for testing the development. This way, the developer can perform his unit test before the consultant tests the new flow.

li.em: Create XXX product with XXX options
Create a SO with this product and put the quantity on XXX
Verify that XXX has been created.

div.p: Since most of the projects you will be implementing are for existing companies, they will likely already have data in their current software that will need to be imported into Odoo, for example an extensive contact list or product catalog. Contacts, products, chart of accounts, categories, etc... are often referred to as "Master Data".

At the very start of each project you will need to discuss with the customer what they would like to do with this information, this will help you better understand what you will need to import. Importing data is not always easy and can be one of the biggest blocking points in moving a project forward. This task aims to give you the tools you need to get your customer's data into Odoo as quickly as possible so you can move onto the more interesting tasks.

b.font: How to prepare for the session:

div.p: Prerequisites:

Review Session 16: "Basic technico-functional knowledge", focusing on what you learned about Odoo's database structure & its fields. This information will help you better understand how to structure the import file and tackle any challenges you may encounter.

Check out this video on how to begin setting up your own import template. While it may be tempting to simply download one that Odoo offers, setting one up on your own will help you understand the intricacies of data importing and better prepare you for more challenging use cases.

While successfully importing the data file is the output at the end of this session, it is more important to understand the changes that were needed to be made in order to get there. This is because not catching these mistakes while in the middle of a project can cost you a lot of time.
As an additional resource to complete this task, be sure to check out the best practices for data imports . This will help you avoid falling into the most common of import traps.
In addition, below is a video explaining some useful concepts that might be of assistance to you, such as XMLID:

p.span: What is expected from you:

div.p: This session is about learning the basic concepts needed to import data and putting them into practice. As your projects become more and more complex over time, and the data volumes larger, you will likely need to switch to writing scripts in order to import their data into Odoo. This will be something that will be covered later on in this course.
With that said, for 80% of your customers a manual import of a data will suffice as long as they are in the following formats: .csv/.xls/.xlsx.
Below are 3 excel files that you need to import into your Odoo test database:

In your Onboarding Exercises
spreadsheet, under the "Basic Imports" tab, note down any and all issues, corrections, and assumptions you have made in order to successfully import the files. Make sure to add an explanation of why you made the changes.
You will be reviewing and correcting this file during the next session with your on-boarder so do not forget to write down any questions that will come up throughout the process.
After having completed these exercises, you are expected to know:

ol.li: What kind of master data needs to be imported in most projects and why;
How to import this data into Odoo;
and how to fix issues within your import files and explain importing basics to your customers.

div.p: In the Basic data import module, we covered importing master data into Odoo. In a real-world implementation, however, imports are rarely that straightforward. Beyond master data, customers often require the migration of more complex datasets, such as inventory adjustments or accounting entries.

We refer to these as “transactional data.” Unlike static master data, transactional data is generated through daily operations and relies on existing master records. For example, you cannot record a stock adjustment for a product that hasn't been imported yet.
This task will give you the necessary tools to make sure that you can advise your customers properly on the way to import transactional data.

font.b: How to prepare for the session:

div.p: - Finished the Basic data import module

- Functional knowledge of excel and using spreadsheet formulas
What is expected of you:
Import the following document into your test database, being sure to write down the changes you made as well as the assumptions required in order to move forward with the data import.
Review the provided data to see the final objective. However, please note that you cannot import this file into Odoo as is; you must first import several other data dependencies.

If time permits, we encourage you to learn how to import a client’s opening balances
in the Accounting application. Remember that the same rules apply: you must establish the necessary master data before attempting to import these entries.

If you have questions or need a refresher, please refer to the "Best Practices for Importing" document. You will review and correct this file during your next session with your on-boarder, so be sure to note any questions that arise during the process.
After having completed this exercise you are expected to know:

ol.li: The differences between transactional data and master data and why import order matters;
How to import transactional data into Odoo and retrieve it later in the database; and
How to run tests before importing transactional data

div.p: Clients are more and more demanding when it comes to having reports and extra BI capabilities. Very often, the default reporting views and dashboards of Odoo are sufficient, but what can we do when the exact group by feature that's expected by the client is nowhere to be found in the existing reporting?
In such cases, as a good Odoo Implementation Methodology project leader, standard solutions should still be the first focus.
The session is divided in two parts :
1. One theoretical session with your Odoo onboarder (1h) :

ul.li: Overview of the standard reporting (from a functional and technical point of view), as well as Accounting Reports building tool
Overview of the standard Dashboard module
Understanding of the link between standard reporting, spreadsheets and dashboard
Introduction to the Odoo 18 Quote Calculator feature

div.p: 2. One practical session with your Odoo onboarder (1h30) : take a look at the Session 24

As seen during this session, Odoo spreadsheet and dashboard is a must-have for any users willing to display and compute data in a very specific way. Thanks to the graphs and filter features, KPI's and Business Intelligence can reach another level and meet most of the client's needs.

div.p: Before turning into a project, a client is a prospect. During the process you will assess the requirements, the scope and the feasibility of the project in order to build an offer to the potential client. Your goal will be to turn this prospect into an actual client.

p.span: Successful projects always start with a proper scope qualification.

ul.li: To improve your estimation skills, both in terms of budget and time needed to carry out an implementation project.
Understand the prospect's needs, as well as his constraints.
Identify functional & technical challenges.
Be able to speak the same language and use the same vocabulary.
Agree on the general scope.
Start building a trustful relationship .
Identify risks or blocking points.
Check that the person you speak to is the right SPoC/Sponsor.
Let the customer speak (active listening) in order to deeply understand the customer's needs. Ask “Why?”.
Try to get the causes and consequences .
Don’t hesitate to expand on the initial scope (eg. If you are speaking about deliveries, ask “what about your stock management ?”)
Don't rush it, take your time.
A global overview of the main business flows and departments.
The key pain points and challenges currently affecting the prospect’s business.
The reasons why the prospect wishes to change ERP.
The current systems used by the prospect.
Concrete examples of daily tasks performed by key users.

div.p: With that information, you can tailor demonstrations to help prospects project themselves in the Odoo solution (use client’s data and take over the client’s main key point).

div.p: Commercial demonstrations are opportunities to :

ul.li: Give the customer a good preview of the tool and potential solution
Verify your understanding of the customer’s needs
Get feedback from the customer, and potentially adjust the demonstration

div.p: Watch the video below containing tips & tricks for a good demo:
A good demonstration must be :

li.p: Customer specific, based on your qualification:

ul.li: use storytelling techniques
show tailored flows
use the prospect’s vocabulary
use data familiar to the prospect (contacts, products …)

Oriented on pain point -> solution -> added value
Example: You waste … time encoding purchase invoice -> the OCR in Odoo automates this process -> which saves … time for your employees that can do more of … instead and increases your revenue/efficiency/…
Push on interactions from the audience (send a mail, decide what to show next, etc.)

div.p: After the demo :

ul.li: Your customer has a better understanding of what Odoo is and how it can solve his pain points.
You have a better understanding of your customer’s needs.
You should always set up the next steps. Don’t lose the momentum.
The demo is also a teaser that should push the client to go for Odoo. We must have some WOW effect.

You may discuss pricing indications using the official pricing page, but any final pricing, discounts, special conditions, or multi-year agreements must always be aligned and validated with the Partner Manager to ensure a consistent and coordinated sales approach. div.p: During the sales process, a demo is given but it's sometimes not sufficient to assess the project's feasibility, for the following reasons (among others):

ul.li: Convoluted and/or specific processes;
Lots of different existing software in the company's IT background;
Knowledge split in different groups of people;
A prospect leaning toward a lot of development.

div.p: Then it might be a good option to propose a ROI analysis before you sell anything else. This chapter will help you understand what is a ROI analysis, why and how we perform it.
The purpose of this chapter is several-fold. We want to:

ul.li: Make you aware that such analysis exists and share our knowledge with you
Show you how the idea of such an analysis needs to be sold to your prospect first;
Show you how it can be used best;
Answer the questions you may have during the group session.

div.p: "ROI" analysis stands for "Return on investment" analysis and is an analysis that aims to measure how much money is earned (thanks to Odoo performance) relative to the amount of money spent on an investment (Odoo subscription).

In concrete terms, ROI analysis enables us to analyze the way customers work today, as well as their functional and technical needs. Based on this, we will develop an Odoo-based solution to show (and convince) the customer that Odoo is the right solution for managing his/her day-to-day activities. The idea is not to replicate the way the customer works today but to improve their processes thanks to Odoo.
Based on this, we draw up a timeline and a budget.

The ROI is still part of the commercial phase, meaning the main goal is to convince the client that Odoo is the best solution. Thanks to the ROI analysis performed prior to the project implementation, we have so far up to 90% of our ROI turning into a project after we present the results.

strong.font: Why do we perform a ROI analysis?

div.p: A ROI analysis is mainly performed for the following reasons:

ul.li: Identify project scope
Understand key pain points
Convince your client
Help to sell Odoo project as an investment and not only a cost
Explain & set up project methodology
Define a proper project budget & planning
Manage internal ressources allocation
Better margin estimation
Make sure my project scope is understood
Get an idea on how to better allocate the time spent by the employees
Understand how the project will go
Manage internal ressources allocation for implementation
Receive a budget for my project
Identify the most impactful features Odoo can bring to the company
Measure the cost/benefit of a customized feature

div.p: The choice of whether or not to do a ROI does not depend solely on the prospect's size. We do ROI's for SME's as well as for MMC's. Both the prospect and you can bring arguments to the table in favor of a ROI analysis. The purpose is to be sure of the feasibility of the project and to understand all its complexity.
Have a look at the video below and then read the extra documentation. We will then discuss it during our group session.
As you can see in the video, Greg explains first why we switched from our previous similar tool (the GAP Analysis) to a more complete ROI encompassing the following aspects on top of the GAP:

ul.li: List inefficiencies,
Saving time and optimization,
What Odoo brings to the company.

div.p: Do note that today we perform what we call “Smart ROI analysis” meaning that we adapt the deliverable to the client needs. We therefore do not always perform the Return part of the ROI (list inefficiencies, saving time and optimization). We only performed it when requested by the client.
A ROI is usually performed in four different phases:
The ROI kickoff ensures that the client understands the methodology, the goal and priorities of such an analysis.

The goal of the AS IS workshops is to understand the way the customer currently works, identify business needs, pain points and risks. We usually organize one AS IS workshop per scope with the right key user.

The goal of the TO BE workshop is to validate the understanding of the processes thanks to a standard demo solution within Odoo. It is important to highlight the fact that you present a draft of the (main) flow you have imagined based on the AS IS and to get feedback from the key users on the solution proposed.

The goal of the result presentation is mainly to discuss the budget and timeline. Usually the key users are not part of this meeting considering that the functional aspects are not the main focus of this presentation.
Keep in mind that performing the ROI is really where you will stand out as a Project Lead: you will mix all your Sales, Functional, and basic Technical aptitudes in the analysis.

ol.li: Sales-wise, you need to maneuver by selling your ideas to the people you interview but also, you will have to present the global ROI (potentially with one of your sales representatives, or along with Odoo) to the prospects decision makers.
Functional-wise, you are going to show your prospect that you know Odoo in and out, and you will sometimes come up with solutions on the spot during the interviews.
Tech-wise, you will be the person explaining and asking your tech team (or Odoo) for some estimates.

div.p: Some people sometimes ask us if this ROI Analysis is done for free. Let's be clear here: it is never free. There are many reasons for that:

ul.li: It is very time-consuming on your side;
Having an ROI Analysis usually diminishes the global effort expected for the implementation. So it already benefits the client if they go with you in the end.

div.p: At the very least, always find a way to monetize it (e.g: make the 5 days ROI analysis a paid service that becomes free IF the client finally goes for the project with you in the end).

After reading this task, you understand better the presales process and how and when to promote the ROI analysis. Your Odoo onboarder will spend some time with you in order to double check your understanding. Keep in mind that this PLO course focuses mainly on smaller implementations.

If after this course, you want to know more about the presales flow for bigger clients as well as about how the OIM is adapted to bigger projects, we recommend you to follow the MMC onboarding course. Contact your partner manager if you have any questions or if you want guidance during the presales process. S.he will be able to help you further in order for you to close the deal.
